source.title: CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents
source.summary: Modern LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenHands share a common inefficiency: they spend much of their token budget finding the file to patch, rather than patching it. On SWE-Bench Verified, a 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, with many calls spent on grep, glob, and view_file during repository exploration. We introduce CodeGrep, a 14B retrieval agent trained end-to-end with GRPO to issue multi-turn parallel grep, glob, and read tool calls and return candidate files to a frozen downstream coding agent. On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep preserves resolve rate while substantially improving efficiency: 27.0% versus 25.8% for the no-retrieval baseline, with 15% fewer rounds and 19% fewer tokens on resolved instances. Across retrievers, downstream utility follows a precision threshold: BM25 with precision 0.375 degrades the agent, Jina with precision 0.445 is neutral, and CodeGrep with precision 0.677 crosses the threshold at which retrieval begins to reduce rollout cost. To enable this study, we mine supervision from 67K open-source agent trajectories using CATM and build a Git-worktree environment for multi-turn agent RL. In our setting, applying the efficiency signal at the advantage layer rather than the reward layer reduces KL drift and translates cleanly into downstream efficiency. We will release the model, training pipeline, RL environment, and evaluation harnesses.

evidence.claim: CodeGrep improves efficiency on SWE-Bench Verified: 15% fewer rounds and 19% fewer tokens on resolved instances while improving resolve rate from 25.8% to 27.0%
evidence.condition: on resolved SWE-Bench Verified instances, downstream agent: OpenHands with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, temperature 0, 100-round max

evidence.claim: Precision threshold for retriever utility: BM25 precision 0.375 degrades agent, Jina 0.445 is neutral, CodeGrep 0.677 crosses threshold for efficiency gain
evidence.condition: precision at which retrieval begins to reduce rollout cost

evidence.claim: Training data from 67,074 open-source OpenHands trajectories using CATM pipeline, yielding 31,977 effective training samples (47.7% retention)
Reward design: applying efficiency signal at advantage layer (v2/v3) reduces KL drift to 0.09-0.15 vs 0.31 for reward layer (v1)
Git-worktree sandbox reduces per-rollout environment setup from minutes to milliseconds, enabling training on single 8x B200 node in ~27 hours

previous_facts.evaluation_context: SWE-Bench Verified (500 instances). Downstream agent: OpenHands (Wang et al., 2024) with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. Temperature 0, 100-round maximum. Training: single 8x B200 node with LoRA, optimizer offload, and vLLM-colocated rollout. Early-stop at step 897 of planned 2000 steps.
previous_facts.limitations: Evidence pack limited to abstract/intro/early design sections; detailed experimental results tables, error analysis, ablation studies, and explicit limitations sections not visible. Index construction cost, repository update overhead, and real-world deployment constraints not described in visible evidence. Precision-only evaluation may miss recall trade-offs.
previous_facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to agent acceleration. CodeGrep demonstrates a clean retrieval-based acceleration approach: training a smaller retrieval agent via RL to reduce redundant Read/Grep operations in larger coding agents. Key insights: (1) RL for tool policies works for code retrieval; (2) efficiency signal belongs at advantage layer, not reward layer; (3) retrievers need high precision (~0.68) to be net-positive for downstream agents; (4) Git-worktree environments enable practical multi-turn agent RL. This validates precision-first retrieval acceleration without heavy indexing infrastructure.
